Purpose NF2 -related schwannomatosis (NF2) is characterized by bilateral vestibular schwannomas (VS) often causing hearing and neurologic deficits, with currently no FDA-approved drug treatment. Pre-clinical studies highlighted the potential of mTORC1 inhibition in delaying schwannoma progression. We conducted a prospective open-label, phase II study of everolimus for progressive VS in NF2 patients and investigated imaging as a potential biomarker predicting effects on growth trajectory. Methods The trial enrolled 12 NF2 patients with progressive VS. Participants received oral everolimus daily for 52 weeks. Brain imaging was obtained quarterly. As primary endpoint, radiographic response (RR) was defined as ≥ 20% decrease in target VS volume. Secondary endpoints included other tumors RR, hearing outcomes, drug safety and quality of life (QOL). Results Eight participants completed the trial and four discontinued the drug early due to significant volumetric VS progression. After 52 weeks of treatment, the median annual VS growth rate decreased from 77.2% at baseline to 29.4%. There was no VS RR and 3 of 8 (37.5%) participants had stable disease. Decreased or unchanged VS volume after 3 months of treatment was predictive of stabilization at 12 months. Seven of eight participants had stable hearing during treatment except one with a decline in word recognition score. Ten of twelve participants reported only minimal changes to their QOL scores. Conclusions Volumetric imaging at 3 months can serve as an early biomarker to predict long-term sensitivity to everolimus treatment. Everolimus may represent a safe treatment option to decrease the growth of NF2-related VS in patients who have stable hearing and neurological condition. TRN: NCT01345136 (April 29, 2011). Keywords Vestibular schwannoma NF2 Everolimus Mammalian target of rapamycin (mTOR) inhibitors Clinical trial Quantitative imaging biomarkers http://dx.doi.org/10.13039/100000090 Congressionally Directed Medical Research Programs W81XWH-12-1-0116 issue-copyright-statement © Springer Science+Business Media, LLC, part of Springer Nature 2024 Introduction NF2 -related schwannomatosis (NF2) (formerly Neurofibromatosis type 2) is a rare autosomal-dominant tumor predisposition syndrome, with an incidence of 1 case in 33,000 live births [ 1 – 3 ]. NF2 patients develop multiple tumors including bilateral vestibular schwannomas (VS), associated with possible bilateral hearing loss, tinnitus, and/or balance disturbances, as well as schwannomas on other cranial and spinal nerves, meningiomas and ependymomas. The tumor burden usually presents early in life, but clinical management can be variable between different patients because of disease heterogeneity in clinical manifestations such as hearing loss and VS growth [ 4 ]. Standard management of NF2 includes conservative observation and microsurgical resection of growing and/or symptomatic tumors. However, surgical resection of VS is associated with a significant rate of hearing loss and carries risks for facial function deficits. While radiotherapy is an alternative therapeutic option in sporadic VS, it is generally not recommended as an early treatment modality for NF2 patients because of a small possible risk of malignant transformation [ 5 ]. Targeted agents have been used for the medical management of NF2-related VS [ 6 – 8 ]. Bevacizumab treatment is associated with high rates of hearing (70%) and tumor (89%) stability [ 9 – 11 ]. However, these VS will almost invariably progress and long-term side effects such as hypertension and proteinuria have been reported [ 12 , 13 ]. Other targeted therapies for VS treatments, such as the endothelial growth factor receptor (EGFR) family kinase inhibitors, lapatinib and erlotinib have been used with limited success [ 14 , 15 ]. Merlin, the NF2 protein, has been identified as a novel negative regulator of mammalian target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1), with functional loss of merlin yielding activation of mTORC1 signaling in NF2-related tumors [ 16 , 17 ]. Our previous study in NF2 mouse schwannoma models showed that long-term inhibition of mTORC1 by rapamycin inhibited tumorigenesis without significant toxicity [ 18 ]. Concomitant with these preclinical studies, we administered everolimus to an index patient with growing VS over a prolonged period resulting in a clinically meaningful growth delay [ 18 ]. Meanwhile, the rapalog everolimus was approved by the FDA for subependymal giant cell astrocytomas associated with tuberous sclerosis, another tumor predisposition syndrome with multiple benign tumors requiring long-term tumor treatment [ 19 ]. Two phase II clinical trials have further evaluated the efficacy of everolimus for progressive VS but only found the best response to be tumor stability [ 20 , 21 ]. Altogether, these data led us to conduct this dual institution open-label phase II clinical trial to evaluate radiographic, hearing and quality of life (QOL) outcomes following everolimus treatment for NF2 patients with progressive VS. The results of the study performed in France were previously published [ 20 ]. Here, we report the results of the US study. In addition to response, we also performed a post-hoc analysis to evaluate whether imaging can serve as an early signature of tumor stabilization.

extracted_data.document_summary: This study investigated everolimus (an mTORC1 inhibitor) as a treatment for progressive NF2-related vestibular schwannomas (VS), evaluating its impact on tumor volume, growth rate, hearing outcomes, and quality of life over 52 weeks. The findings indicate that 3-month volumetric imaging can serve as an early biomarker to predict long-term sensitivity to everolimus, which demonstrated a cytostatic effect by decreasing VS growth rates, stabilizing tumors, and improving time to progression, while generally maintaining hearing and quality of life, despite not achieving significant tumor shrinkage in all cases.

treatment_details.therapy_type: Everolimus (mTORC1 inhibitor), with some cases also involving Bevacizumab as a subsequent or alternative treatment.
treatment_details.dose_specificity: Oral everolimus was administered daily for 52 weeks (12 months) to NF2 patients with progressive VS. Adult participants (18+) received 10 mg/day, and adolescents (16-17) received 3 mg/day. Doses could be reduced (e.g., to 5 mg/day for adults) due to toxicity, such as grade 3+ or grade 2 oral ulcers. While no formal dose-response comparisons were reported, the treatment period was continuous for 52 weeks, with some patients re-challenged with everolimus after discontinuation, and others receiving bevacizumab if everolimus failed to control growth.

analyzed_biomarkers.biomarker_name: Vestibular Schwannoma (VS) volume and growth rate
analyzed_biomarkers.measured_tissue_or_fluid: Brain (imaging of VS); Tumor tissue (measured via MRI)
analyzed_biomarkers.activity_type: Radiographic response; Tumor Volume Measurement; Rate of Tumor Growth; Volumetric analysis (imaging)

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Lower growth rate; stable disease for a subset; decreased or unchanged volume predictive of stabilization.
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Median annual VS growth rate decreased from 77.2% at baseline to 29.4% after 52 weeks. No VS radiographic response (defined as ">= 20% decrease") was observed; 3 of 8 (37.5%) participants had stable disease. Decreased or unchanged VS volume after 3 months of treatment (or an annualized VS growth rate < 1%) was predictive of stabilization at 12 months. Baseline median target VS volume was 5.7 cm³ (IQR 1.1 to 7.8), decreasing to 2.6 cm³ (IQR 1.1 to 6.4) after 12 months. Best tumor response was -14% in the first 3 months (Participant 7). Stable disease showed an average target VS volume increase of 5.7% at 12 months, compared to 38% at baseline. Everolimus discontinuation led to tumor progression (e.g., Participant 1: 30% increase in 3 months; Participant 7: 64% increase in 3 months; Participant 9: 26% increase in 1 month), while re-challenge led to growth stabilization (+6% growth for Participant 9). Any increase (<20%) at 3 months predicted progression (>20%) at 12 months. Patients on bevacizumab alone showed some tumor shrinkage and overall tumor stability. Growth rate was reduced in seven patients after 12 months.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Indication of tumor proliferation, progression, and overall disease burden; measures rate of tumor cell proliferation.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Everolimus treatment for progressive NF2-related vestibular schwannoma; everolimus discontinuation; everolimus re-challenge; bevacizumab treatment.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Serves as an early biomarker to predict long-term sensitivity to everolimus treatment, indicates treatment efficacy in slowing tumor growth, disease progression, and prognosis; cytostatic effect of everolimus on tumor growth.

measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Participant 1 showed a 23% increase in 3 months (13.5 cm³) after everolimus discontinuation. Participant 8 had a 6.2% reduction in the contralateral non-target VS, showing stabilization of -6% at 12 months. Overall, 11 of 15 non-target tumors were stable during the study period.

analyzed_biomarkers.biomarker_name: Hearing outcomes (Pure Tone Audiometry (PTA) and Word Recognition Score (WRS))
analyzed_biomarkers.activity_type: Functional assessment; Clinical Measurement (hearing test); Audiometric measurement; Clinical observation

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Stable or improved for most; decline for some.
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: PTA remained stable or improved in all target ears of the 8 participants who completed the 12-month study. Participant 8 showed PTA improvement from 60dB at baseline to 52.5dB at 12-month follow-up. WRS remained stable or improved for 7 of 8 participants, with Participant 9's WRS improving from 96% to 100% at month 15 after resuming everolimus. However, Participant 7 experienced marked WRS deterioration from 58% to 20% over drug treatment, decreasing to 0% after drug withdrawal. Participant 1 experienced rapid decreased hearing in the contralateral ear one month after everolimus discontinuation, while Participant 8 had concurrent hearing recovery in the associated ear with a 6.2% reduction in non-target VS.

analyzed_biomarkers.core_biological_function: Indicator of auditory neurological function; measures hearing thresholds and speech understanding ability; auditory perception.
analyzed_biomarkers.relevant_activity_context: Everolimus treatment for progressive NF2-related vestibular schwannoma; Everolimus discontinuation; Everolimus re-challenge; 12-months of everolimus study treatment.
analyzed_biomarkers.performance_or_health_indicator: Indicates the impact of everolimus treatment on hearing stability, suggesting suitability for patients with stable hearing; indicates hearing preservation and potential benefit of treatment on auditory function; indicates speech comprehension preservation and potential benefit; indicates hearing loss or recovery associated with tumor changes and treatment status.

measured_effect.direction_of_change: Minimal overall changes; worsening in specific domains.
measured_effect.magnitude_quantification: Ten of twelve participants reported only minimal changes to their overall QOL scores. However, specific SF-36 domains showed mean worsening over 12 months: Emotional role (-19.4), Fatigue (-10.2), General health (-19.2), Social function (-11.5), and Pain (-11.5).
